# Gear-Box Fault Detection

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** Cepstrum analysis — separating source and transmission-path contributions in machinery vibration.
**Chapter:** [2 — Frequency Domain](../chap2.qmd)

---

## Background

A rotating gear-box produces vibration at the gear-mesh frequency $f_\text{mesh} = N_\text{teeth} \times f_\text{shaft}$ and its harmonics. A bearing fault modulates these harmonics at the fault frequency $f_\text{fault}$, creating a comb-like family of sidebands in the power spectrum. The **cepstrum** lifts the log-spectrum into the "quefrency" domain, turning multiplicative source–path convolutions into additive sums and making the sideband spacing (i.e., $f_\text{fault}$) directly readable as a peak location.

## Key idea

The real cepstrum is the inverse DFT of the log power spectrum:

$$
c[\tau] = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\left\{\ln |\hat{X}(f)|^2\right\}
$$

A family of harmonics spaced $\Delta f$ apart in frequency becomes a single peak at quefrency $\tau = 1/\Delta f$ in the cepstrum. Bearing defect frequencies are thus directly readable without needing to identify individual harmonics.

The **liftering** operation removes the low-quefrency structural response, isolating the fault signature:

$$
c_\text{liftered}[\tau] = c[\tau] \cdot w[\tau], \quad w[\tau] = \begin{cases} 0 & \tau < \tau_0 \\ 1 & \tau \geq \tau_0 \end{cases}
$$

## Code

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.io import loadmat

# Load CWRU bearing dataset (48 kHz, drive-end accelerometer)
mat = loadmat('docs/Data/gearbox/CWRU_48k_load_1_CNN_data.npz')
fs = 48_000
x = mat['drive_end_fault'].ravel()[:fs * 4]   # 4-second snippet

# PSD via Welch
f, Pxx = scipy.signal.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=4096, scaling='density')

# Real cepstrum
log_psd = np.log(Pxx + 1e-30)
cepstrum = np.fft.irfft(log_psd).real
quefrency = np.arange(len(cepstrum)) / fs * 1e3   # ms

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6))

axes[0].semilogy(f / 1e3, Pxx)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Frequency (kHz)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('PSD (m²/s⁴/Hz)')
axes[0].set_title('Power Spectrum — bearing fault sidebands')

axes[1].plot(quefrency[1:500], cepstrum[1:500], lw=0.8)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Quefrency (ms)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Cepstrum amplitude')
axes[1].set_title('Real Cepstrum — fault period visible as peak')

plt.tight_layout()
```

## Result

<div class="gallery-result">
![Cepstrum of gear-box vibration revealing bearing defect quefrency peak](../Figure/figure_cepstrum.png)
</div>

The cepstrum peak at a quefrency corresponding to the ball-pass outer-race frequency is clearly visible, even though the individual sidebands in the power spectrum are hard to count by eye. Liftering above the structural quefrency leaves only the fault signature.

## Healthy vs. faulty: the fault as a taller rahmonic

The clearest way to *see* a fault is to overlay the healthy and faulty recordings. Using the [SpectraQuest gear-box dataset](https://github.com/jiutongzhao/Time-Series-Data-Analysis/blob/main/Data/gearbox_spectraquest.npz) shipped with this book ($f_s = 66.7$ kHz), the fault modulates the gear mesh at the shaft rotation rate ($f_\text{shaft}\approx 77$ Hz), sprinkling a family of sidebands spaced $77$ Hz apart around the mesh harmonics. In the power spectrum (left) the faulty trace sits well above the healthy one and grows a forest of extra sideband peaks; the cepstrum (right) collapses that whole comb into a single **rahmonic** at quefrency $1/f_\text{shaft}\approx 12.9$ ms — which stands markedly taller for the faulty gear precisely because it carries more sidebands.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

d = np.load('Data/gearbox_spectraquest.npz', allow_pickle=True)
fs = int(d['fs']); healthy = d['healthy'].astype(float); broken = d['broken'].astype(float)

def analyse(x):
    f, P = signal.welch(x, fs=fs, nperseg=8192, scaling='density')
    c = np.fft.irfft(np.log(P + 1e-30)).real          # real cepstrum
    q = np.arange(c.size) / fs                         # quefrency [s]
    return f, P, q, c

fh, Ph, qh, ch = analyse(healthy)
fb, Pb, qb, cb = analyse(broken)
q_shaft = 1 / 77.3                                     # shaft-rate quefrency (~12.9 ms)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 3.6), layout='constrained')

band = (fh > 3500) & (fh < 6500)                       # zoom on a mesh-harmonic band
ax[0].semilogy(fh[band], Ph[band], lw=0.8, label='healthy', zorder=3)  # healthy on top
ax[0].semilogy(fb[band], Pb[band], lw=0.8, label='faulty',  zorder=2)
ax[0].set_xlabel('frequency [Hz]'); ax[0].set_ylabel('PSD [arb.]')
ax[0].set_title('power spectrum — mesh sidebands'); ax[0].legend()

m = (qh > 1.2e-3) & (qh < 0.022)
ax[1].plot(qh[m]*1e3, ch[m], lw=0.9, label='healthy', zorder=3)  # healthy on top
ax[1].plot(qb[m]*1e3, cb[m], lw=0.9, label='faulty',  zorder=2)
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    ax[1].axvline(k*q_shaft*1e3, ls=':', lw=0.7, color='0.5')  # shaft rahmonics
ax[1].set_xlabel('quefrency [ms]'); ax[1].set_ylabel('cepstrum amplitude [arb.]')
ax[1].set_title('cepstrum — shaft-rate rahmonic'); ax[1].legend()

plt.savefig('figure_gearbox_cepstrum_compare.png', dpi=200, bbox_inches='tight')
```

<div class="gallery-result">
![Healthy (blue) vs. faulty (red) gear-box vibration. Left: in a mesh-harmonic band the faulty spectrum lifts above the healthy one and grows extra sidebands spaced at the shaft rate. Right: the cepstrum turns that sideband comb into one rahmonic at $1/f_\text{shaft}\approx 12.9$ ms (and its multiples at 6.5 and 19.4 ms) — taller for the faulty gear because it has more sidebands to accumulate.](../Figure/figure_gearbox_cepstrum_compare.png)
</div>

A single scalar — the height of the shaft-rate rahmonic — thus separates a healthy gear from a faulty one, without having to count sidebands by eye. This mirrors the classic comparison in Siemens' [*Cepstrum Analysis*](https://community.sw.siemens.com/s/article/Cepstrum-Analysis) tutorial (their Figure 11), reproduced here from this book's own SpectraQuest data.
